**Digital euro trilogue faces make-or-break round on merchant fees**

*Merchant fee methodology and business holding limits remain unresolved as the Irish EU presidency targets a political agreement on November 18, with the ECB's 2029 issuance timeline at stake.*

EU negotiators are attempting to close a deal on the digital euro regulation on November 18 after four months of trilogue talks between the European Parliament, the Council and the Commission. The Irish presidency, which chairs the negotiations for member states, has set the date as its target for a political agreement. If reached, lawyers would finalise the text and both institutions would vote in 2027. A miss would push the process into a new Council presidency and jeopardise the ECB's planned 2029 first issuance.

The central sticking point is how merchant fees are calculated. Both institutions want uniform fee caps across the euro area, starting with a transitional model and later moving to cost-based charges plus a margin. France is opposing a "no worse off" clause sought by Parliament, under which digital euro transaction fees would have to be at least as favourable as those for other existing payment types. A French finance ministry source said the reference to other payments raises problems because it would include domestic European schemes, which charge less than international card networks. The two sides also diverge on business holding limits: Parliament favours a near-total ban on holdings by legal persons written into the regulation, while the Council would leave the matter to the ECB.

Piero Cipollone, the ECB executive board member leading the digital euro project, told Parliament's economic affairs committee on November 10 that legislative delay could postpone introduction beyond 2029 and deepen Europe's dependence on non-EU payment providers. The ECB plans a 12-month pilot starting in the second half of 2027 with 36 selected payment service providers, but can only set an issuance date after the regulation is adopted.

**Milan court places Revolut under year-long judicial oversight for AML failures**

*The order exposes the gap between rapid customer growth across EU borders and the compliance infrastructure needed to support it, with Italy's fifth-largest bank by customer numbers found to have filed none of the suspicious transaction reports that other banks flagged on the same individuals.*

A Milan court has placed Revolut Bank UAB's Italian branch under judicial administration for one year after finding that at least 24 individuals under investigation or convicted of money laundering and organised crime offences had moved approximately €41.9 million through the bank's accounts between 2021 and 2026. Other banks filed 265 suspicious transaction reports on those same individuals over the period; Revolut filed none. The court cited "serious deficiencies" in the bank's anti-money laundering controls and appointed two judicial administrators with broad oversight and inspection powers.

Revolut must now implement a 15-point remediation plan, appoint an internal liaison officer within five days and submit a detailed compliance action plan within 60 days. The administrators will file a preliminary report within 30 days and a full assessment within 90. The measure is preventive rather than punitive under Italian law – Revolut is not under criminal investigation, and its Italian retail and commercial services continue to operate normally.

The ruling follows an €11.5 million fine from Italy's competition authority in April and a separate 2024 inspection by Milan's Guardia di Finanza into Revolut Digital Assets Europe, the entity handling cryptocurrency services for European users. With more than five million customers in Italy, Revolut is the country's largest foreign bank by client numbers. The case underscores a recurring tension in European financial services: digital banks licensed in one member state and operating across the bloc through passporting can grow their customer base far faster than their local compliance operations.

**Starling founder Anne Boden launches agent-native banking venture Lockwood**

*The new UK challenger, designed from scratch for AI agents to initiate payments within user-set limits, plans to seek an e-money licence in 2027 before converting to a full bank.*

Anne Boden, founder of Starling Bank, is building Lockwood, a current account platform designed for customers who delegate spending decisions to AI agents. Boden told The Sunday Times the venture would be "built by agents, to serve customers that want to use agents, and then be defended by agents". She is self-funding the early stage with proceeds from selling her roughly 5% Starling stake.

Lockwood will offer a free current account but no lending or savings products, earning revenue from interest on deposits. It will seek authorisation as an electronic money institution in 2027 before converting to a full banking licence, with a planned launch in 2028 and a target of one million customers in its first year. Boden said she also plans to convene a working party of banks and regulators to establish how agentic banking should operate.

The venture arrives as major UK banks remain reluctant to grant AI agents access to customer accounts over concerns about unauthorised transactions. By building agent access and transaction controls into the infrastructure from the outset rather than retrofitting them, Boden is betting that the next generation of digital banking will be shaped by how well institutions accommodate machine-initiated payments, not just human ones.

**Capital One warns banks are becoming default absorber of online fraud losses**

*Liability frameworks in payments increasingly concentrate fraud costs on banks rather than the platforms where fraud originates, a tension sharpened by the UK's mandatory reimbursement rules.*

Capital One has warned that banks are becoming the "default shock absorber" for online fraud, bearing losses that originate on platforms and marketplaces beyond their control. The argument, made through Open Banking Expo, points to a structural imbalance in how fraud liability is distributed across the payments chain.

The warning resonates in the UK context, where the Payment Systems Regulator's mandatory reimbursement regime for authorised push payment fraud has been in force since late 2024. Monzo reported an 85% surge in fraud reimbursement costs under the regime in the first quarter of 2025, and UK fraud losses have climbed to £1.3 billion. Banks argue they are absorbing costs for scams that originate on social media platforms, online marketplaces and telecommunications networks, none of which currently bear equivalent liability.

The bank's framing adds a transatlantic voice to a debate that is intensifying in both the UK and Europe. The European Commission's instant payments regulation requires verification of payee but does not impose the same reimbursement obligations that the UK has adopted. How liability is shared between banks, platforms and payment providers remains one of the most contested policy questions in payments regulation.
